newsitem.title: USA: Majors boost upstream and chemicals, cut downstream.
newsitem.headline: Majors boost upstream and chemicals, cut downstream.

text.p: International energy companies are to increase spending on exploration, production and chemicals, but most are cutting downstream budgets, executives told the Howard Weil energy conference.

Increased upstream spending is aimed at meeting forecast demand for energy of 150 million barrels of oil equivalent per day in the year 2010, two-thirds of which will have to come from new discoveries.
"We are now becoming a company which relies mainly on the upstream sector for its profits," Total SA chief executive Thierry Desmarest told the conference on Tuesday.

Total aims to increase its annual output to one million barrels of energy equivalent by the year 2000 from 762 million in 1996 and has already raised the portion of its earnings from upstream operations to over 70 percent of operating income in 1996 from less than half in 1993.
A Howard Weil survey of 14 major energy companies showed that of the 128 projects planned, 91 were in the upstream sector.
Where Total is remaining in the downtream sector, it is concentrating on high growth emerging markets and has already cut some U.S. capacity and reduced spending in western Europe.
"We are seeing refining margins in western Europe at the same depressed level as last year," Desmarest said.
Exxon Corp also is looking for new reserves and expects to add one billion plus barrels a year every year from now on. It is now a major player in the former Soviet Union.
"We already have 10 billion barrels of reserves in the FSU and are in exclusive negotiations to acquire another 10 billion plus," chief executive Lee Raymond.
In the chemicals sector, both Exxon and Total plan major expansions.
Exxon, which recently announced it was to build a major chemicals complex in Singapore, plans to increase assets in Asia Pacific to 30 percent of chemical plant by 2000 from 25 percent at present.
Capital employed in Total's chemical business will rise to 22 percent of 100 billion francs in 2000 from 21 percent of 78 billion in 1995.
It also plans 3.0 billion francs in acquisitions in the chemicals sector through to the year 2000 in an effort to raise sales for the division to 30 billion francs by 2000 from 24.6 billion in 1996.
According to Howard Weil analyst Bud Tower, only one company expects growth in all three sectors, upstream, chemicals and downstream, and that is Phillips Petroleum Co.

Phillips is bucking the trend with an increase in spending on refining to $140 million in 1997 from $109 million in 1996 and aims for a large increase in chemicals, plastics and natural gas liquids to $350 million from $205 million.

"On chemicals we have have been cautious overseas but we do plan to globalise this business and are looking at the Middle East, Canada and Venezuela," chief executive Wayne Allen told Reuters in an interview.
Allen aims to raise the proportion of Phillips' non-cyclical chemicals income to 25-30 percent in the next ten years from 10- 15 percent now.
Allen said that while downstream oil operations were not meeting the cost of capital, it was premature to talk of a strategic alliance.
"A lot of companies do not like integration, we prefer to be highly integrated. A cent or two makes all the difference," Allen said.
